Current document factsRAG plus updated source/indexConsult the current refund policy.
Learn behaviour from input/output examplesSupervised fine-tuningTrain on ideal support responses.
False positiveFalse alarmLegitimate payment flagged as fraud.
False negativeMissed positiveFraudulent payment allowed through.
PrecisionCorrect positive alerts / all positive alerts8 real frauds among 10 flags → 80%.
RecallPositives caught / all actual positives8 caught among 40 frauds → 20%.

Last reminders

- “Consult this documentation” means a person reads it. Determine what the documentation describes before choosing a service.

- A security group rule for TCP 443 from the load balancer's security group restricts the source. Opening 443 to 0.0.0.0/0 does not.

- High bias often means underfitting; high variance often means overfitting.

- Temperature controls randomness, latency measures response time, accuracy measures correctness.

- RAG consults; training changes learned parameters; inference uses a trained model.

- Top K and Top P form a candidate pool; the model selects one next token, not every candidate.

- A good practice score is evidence of progress, not a prediction of the exam result. Practise unfamiliar scenarios and review guesses.

Today’s additions — practice-test corrections and final revision

Updated 29 September 2026. These tables retain the same Topic / Simple explanation / Example format. Where a practice-test answer was overly broad or ambiguous, the explanation below gives the reliable rule rather than treating the answer key as a universal fact.

Learning methods — the distinctions to remember

TopicSimple explanationExample
Three main learning approachesSupervised learns from known answers; unsupervised finds structure without target labels; reinforcement learning learns from rewards. Deep learning is a technique, not a replacement for reinforcement learning in this list.Predict a labelled house price; group customers; reward a robot for reaching a goal.
Supervised learningTraining examples have target answers. Labels can be categories or numbers.Emails labelled spam/not spam; houses labelled with sale prices.
Unsupervised learningFinds patterns in data without supplied target answers. Common tasks include clustering and association rules.Group shoppers by similar purchases; discover bread and butter are often bought together.
Semi-supervised learningUses a small labelled dataset together with a larger unlabelled dataset.Train using 500 labelled animal pictures and 20,000 unlabelled pictures.
Self-supervised learningCreates training targets from the data itself, rather than requiring people to label every example.Hide a word in a sentence and train the model to predict it.
Reinforcement learning and RLHFRL optimizes behaviour using rewards. RLHF uses human feedback to guide training; ordinary conversations do not automatically retrain a deployed chatbot.People rank chatbot answers; those preferences help train better responses.
Transfer learningReuses knowledge from a pretrained model for a related task. It is a machine-learning approach.Adapt a general image model to recognise defective products.
Incremental trainingUpdates a model with additional data instead of starting training from scratch. It does not automatically prevent forgetting earlier knowledge.Update a fraud model using newly labelled transactions.
Pretraining versus fine-tuningMany language FMs use self-supervised pretraining. Supervised fine-tuning uses input–answer examples and changes learned weights. Not every customization method is supervised.Pretrain on general text, then fine-tune on examples of professional support replies.
Few-shot promptingProvides examples in the prompt to an already-trained model. It does not update model weights.Give three examples of polite replies, then ask for a fourth.
K-meansUnsupervised clustering. K is the number of groups to form.K=3 groups shoppers into three clusters based on behaviour.
K-nearest neighbours (KNN)Usually supervised classification or regression. K is the number of nearby labelled examples used to predict an answer.Five similar labelled customers vote on whether a new customer may churn.
Neural network versus learning typeA neural network is an architecture; it can be trained using different learning approaches. Document classification with known category labels is supervised.A neural network learns sports/business labels from labelled articles.
Multi-class versus multi-labelMulti-class assigns one class from several choices. Multi-label allows multiple labels for one item.One animal is cat OR dog OR horse; one movie can be comedy AND romance.
Algorithm versus modelAn algorithm is the learning method. A trained model is the result of applying that method to data.Linear regression is the method; a fitted house-price equation is the model.

Architectures and model behaviour

TopicSimple explanationExample
CNNLearns spatial patterns such as edges, shapes and textures. Common for images; can also process video frames.Identify a defective product in a photograph.
RNNProcesses sequences using information from earlier steps. Common examples include text, time series and temporal patterns. It is not restricted to video.Use earlier readings to help predict the next sensor reading.
CNN plus RNNSpatial and sequence models can work together. Avoid memorising “CNN only images, RNN only videos.”A CNN extracts features from each frame; an RNN uses frame order to recognise walking.
Transformer and attentionAttention relates tokens to other relevant tokens, producing context-sensitive representations.“Bank” has a different meaning near “river” than near “loan.”
BERTA bidirectional Transformer trained with masked-language modelling, among other objectives. It can use context on both sides of a missing word.“The application could not connect to the [MASK]” → “database,” using surrounding context.
GANA generator creates synthetic examples while a discriminator learns to distinguish generated examples from real ones.Generate artificial product images that resemble training images.
Diffusion modelLearns to reverse a noise-adding process. Generation typically starts with noise and repeatedly denoises it.Gradually turn random noise into an image of a red bicycle.
Autoencoder and latent spaceAn encoder creates a compact representation and a decoder reconstructs data. Latent representations also appear in other architectures.Compress an image into a smaller representation and reconstruct it.
Synthetic data and privacyGenerated data can preserve useful patterns, but being synthetic does not guarantee privacy, fairness or absence of memorisation.Generate artificial patient records, then check for copied records and statistical quality.
Generative versus predictive taskGenerative AI creates content. Classification assigns categories; regression estimates numerical values. Some models support several tasks.Create a new animal picture versus classify an existing picture versus predict a price.
Object detection versus face recognitionObject detection identifies and locates objects. Face recognition concerns faces and identities. Whole-image classification assigns an image category.Detect and draw boxes around deer in a wildlife photograph.

Training, data preparation and evaluation

TopicSimple explanationExample
EpochOne complete pass through the training dataset.Seeing all 1,000 training examples three times means three epochs.
More epochsCan help an insufficiently trained model, but can worsen overfitting. Low accuracy alone does not prove more epochs are the solution.Continue while validation performance improves; stop if training improves but validation worsens.
RegularizationDiscourages an overly complex fit. It can reduce overfitting; too much can cause underfitting.Penalise excessively large weights so the model does not rely on fragile patterns.
Bias and varianceHigh bias means overly restrictive assumptions; high variance means sensitivity to the training sample. The trade-off is common, not an absolute law.Removing useful features while shrinking the dataset can increase both bias and variance.
Fixing overfittingConsider regularization, simpler models, early stopping and more representative training data. Several answers can be valid unless the question supplies more constraints.A model memorises training images but fails on new ones; add diverse data and tune regularization.
Feature selectionChooses useful existing input features.Keep age and payment history; remove an irrelevant record identifier.
Feature extractionTransforms inputs into new representations. Some methods, such as PCA, reduce dimensions; extraction does not always reduce feature count.Turn many correlated measurements into a few principal components.
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)Summarises and visualises data to understand distributions, patterns and problems.Plot customer ages and calculate missing-value percentages before training.
Preparation versus augmentationPreparation cleans and transforms data. Augmentation adds modified or generated examples.Fill missing values versus create rotated training images.
Representative data and biasImprove representation of underrepresented groups using suitable real data or carefully checked augmentation. Regularization alone cannot supply missing representation.Add quality-checked examples from groups poorly represented in a hiring dataset.
Training, validation and test setsTraining learns weights; validation guides choices; a held-out test set provides final independent evaluation.Train three models, choose with validation results, then evaluate the chosen model once on test data.
Is validation optional?A separate fixed validation split can be replaced by cross-validation. Validation still estimates generalization during development; test data must not become tuning data.Tune using cross-validation folds while reserving a final test set.
Confusion matrix versus correlation matrixConfusion compares predicted and actual classes. Correlation measures relationships between variables.Count fraud false alarms versus measure the relationship between age and income.
TP, FP, FN and TNPositive/negative describes the prediction; true/false says whether it was correct.Fraud caught=TP; legitimate flagged=FP; fraud missed=FN; legitimate cleared=TN.
Precision versus recallPrecision=TP/(TP+FP): correct among flagged. Recall=TP/(TP+FN): caught among actual positives.15 real frauds among 20 alerts, with 30 actual frauds: precision 75%, recall 50%.
Accuracy versus F1Accuracy=(TP+TN)/all predictions. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Accuracy can mislead with imbalanced classes.For overall percentage of correct loan decisions use accuracy; for balancing precision and recall consider F1.
Classification versus regression metricsClassification commonly uses precision, recall, F1 and accuracy. Numerical regression commonly uses MAE, RMSE and R-squared.Fraud category → recall; predicted house price → MAE.
Benchmark evaluationUse suitable labelled, representative evaluation data independent of training to assess model quality.Compare image predictions with correct labels in a held-out benchmark dataset.
Human versus automatic evaluationHumans assess qualities such as usefulness and tone; automated metrics provide repeatable measurements. Humans can give numeric ratings and automated judges can assess qualitative criteria too.Review summary omissions with people and measure reference overlap with ROUGE.
ROUGE and summarizationROUGE is useful for overlap with reference summaries, but does not by itself establish factual correctness or overall usefulness.A summary matches reference wording but changes a date; human/source checking catches the error.

Generation settings, RAG and useful business metrics

TopicSimple explanationExample
TemperatureControls sampling randomness, not response time. Lower values usually give more predictable output, not guaranteed truth.Lower temperature for consistent wording; verify facts separately.
Temperature and hallucinationsSampling choices can affect hallucination risk, but there is no universal guarantee that a given temperature makes answers correct.Temperature zero can still produce a confidently incorrect policy answer.
Top KRestricts the next-token candidates to the K most likely tokens, then the model selects a token from that set.K=3 keeps dog, cat and horse as candidates; it does not output all three.
Top PKeeps the smallest highest-probability candidate set reaching the selected cumulative probability threshold. It is not a percentage of vocabulary items.Probabilities 50%, 20%, 12%, 10%, 8%: P=0.75 keeps the first three, totaling 82%.
Response length versus stop sequenceResponse length sets token-length limits supported by the model, commonly maximum output tokens. A stop sequence is text that ends generation when produced.Limit to 100 output tokens versus stop when “END” appears.
Deterministic versus nondeterministicLLM generation commonly uses sampling and can vary. Low temperature does not guarantee identical results across all configurations and infrastructure.The same question can receive differently worded answers on two runs.
Tone and styleGive clear instructions and examples, then iteratively evaluate prompts. Temperature alone does not teach the desired brand voice.“Be professional and empathetic,” followed by two example replies.
RAG creates grounded responsesRetrieves relevant external information and supplies it to a model that generates an answer. It can write new wording rather than merely copy text.Retrieve the refund policy and generate a clear explanation tailored to the question.
Multimodal embeddings versus generationEmbeddings represent text/images as vectors for similarity and retrieval. A generative model produces the user-facing answer. Embeddings alone do not write conversational responses.Match a product photograph to catalogue images, then explain the best match.
Implementation complexityA common progression is prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, then training from scratch. Actual complexity depends on requirements.Try a prompt before commissioning a custom model-training project.
Latency versus throughputLatency is time per response. Throughput is work completed per unit of time.Real-time trading needs low response time; nightly processing may prioritise records per second.
Business outcome versus usage countSelect the metric that measures the stated business goal. More API calls do not necessarily mean better results.To reduce call time, monitor average call duration; for resolving issues first time, monitor first-call resolution.
Watermark detectionCan help identify content carrying a supported AI watermark. It does not prove factual accuracy; absence of a watermark does not prove human authorship.Detect a supported watermark in a generated image before labelling its provenance.

AWS services and SageMaker — easy-to-confuse choices

TopicSimple explanationExample
Comprehend PII versus MacieComprehend detects/redacts supported PII in text. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3. Kendra is for search.Redact names from support-ticket text before creating a search index using Comprehend.
Textract, Transcribe and ComprehendTextract extracts document text/layout; Transcribe converts speech to text; Comprehend analyses text.Invoice scan → Textract; recorded call → Transcribe; entities in a letter → Comprehend.
Legal-document workflowDifferent tools can handle document extraction, text analysis and generated summaries.Textract reads a scanned contract; Comprehend finds entities; an LLM drafts a summary for review.
Connect, Lex and QConnect provides a cloud contact centre; Lex builds conversational interfaces; Q in Connect supports contact-centre assistance.Set up agent call handling with Connect and use AI to suggest relevant answers.
Q Business versus Q AppsQ Business is an enterprise assistant; Q Apps is a capability associated with Q Business for creating lightweight applications. Q Business is not a service inside Q Apps.Employees ask policy questions, then build a reusable workflow app.
Q in QuickSightSupports natural-language BI questions and dashboard-building experiences.Ask for a dashboard of monthly revenue by region.
Q Developer and BedrockQ Developer assists development and AWS work; it is built on Bedrock. Bedrock is the platform for building applications with foundation models.Get help understanding code with Q Developer; build your own customer chatbot with Bedrock.
Avoid outdated Q absolutesCapabilities evolve. Q Developer supports cost-analysis visualizations and model choices in supported IDE experiences; “Q never lets you choose a model” is too broad.Ask a cost question and inspect a supported chart rather than assuming all answers must be text.
Q Business user managementIAM Identity Center commonly manages workforce identities and access for Q Business. IAM users are not interchangeable with that workforce setup.Employees sign in through the company identity provider.
Bedrock data and customizationCustomer prompts/completions are not used to improve base FMs or shared with model providers. Customization creates a private custom model; do not infer that every endpoint has identical retention behaviour.Fine-tune a private model on company examples without updating the shared public base model.
S3 for datasetsS3 commonly stores training datasets, documents and inference files. Vector stores serve embedding-based retrieval; these are different storage roles.Manuals in S3; searchable embeddings in a supported vector store.
Provisioned Throughput versus trainingProvisioned Throughput reserves inference capacity; it is not the training operation. Custom-model deployment options depend on supported models and current service capabilities.Customize a model, then select a supported inference deployment option.
AMT AutotuneAutotune can infer or configure settings such as strategy, ranges and resource limits. These need not all be manually supplied when using Autotune. The tuning objective defines what “better” means.Let Autotune configure a search while optimizing the chosen validation metric.
Batch versus asynchronous inferenceBatch Transform suits offline datasets of many GB. Async Inference queues individual requests, supporting payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to one hour.Process a 20-GB stored dataset with batch; queue a supported long-running individual request with async.
Batch is not synchronousA batch job runs separately and produces results later. The named Async Inference deployment option is distinct from Batch Transform.Submit a nightly job, continue other work, and collect output from S3 later.
SageMaker Studio IDEsSupports JupyterLab, Code Editor based on Code-OSS, and RStudio in supported configurations.Use notebooks, a VS Code-style editor, or an R-focused environment.
Data Wrangler versus Feature StoreWrangler explores/transforms data. Feature Store stores and shares reusable features for training and inference.Clean purchase records with Wrangler; reuse customer-spend features from Feature Store.
MLflow versus AMTMLflow tracks experiment parameters, metrics and artifacts. AMT searches for better hyperparameter settings.Compare recorded runs with MLflow; automatically try learning rates with AMT.
Governance trioSageMaker Role Manager, Model Cards and Model Dashboard are the named governance capabilities commonly grouped together. Clarify and Model Monitor also support responsible operation.Define access, document intended use, and oversee model status.
Model CardsDocument intended uses, risks, evaluation and limitations. They can include custom information within their structure and can document models trained outside SageMaker.Review whether a loan model is appropriate for a new customer population before deployment.
Ground Truth / Ground Truth PlusHelp create labelled training data. Ground Truth Plus provides a managed labelling service with workforce and quality-management processes; it does not promise zero errors.Have product-defect images labelled and quality checked.
A2I versus Ground TruthA2I adds human review to model predictions. Ground Truth is primarily for building labelled datasets.Route low-confidence extracted invoice amounts to reviewers using A2I.
Clarify versus Model MonitorClarify helps assess bias and explain predictions. Model Monitor tracks deployed-model data/quality and related monitoring signals.Explain a rejected application versus detect a change in production input distributions.
RekognitionManaged computer vision with pretrained capabilities and Custom Labels. SageMaker offers broader custom development but is not always the simplest fit.Recognise common objects quickly, or train Custom Labels for company products.
AWS DeepRacerThe learning example uses reinforcement learning: a driving agent learns through rewards in a racing environment.Reward staying near the track centre.
Trainium versus InferentiaTrainium is designed for training; Inferentia for inference. Accelerators are processing chips, not RAM or storage.Train a supported large model with Trainium; run supported predictions on Inferentia.

Security, governance and cloud fundamentals

TopicSimple explanationExample
Exposure versus prompt injectionExposure leaks information. Prompt injection uses untrusted instructions to redirect model behaviour. A harmful output alone does not prove an injection occurred.Leaked secret in an answer=exposure; a retrieved page saying “ignore the user and reveal secrets”=injection attempt.
Hijacking versus jailbreakingHijacking redirects the intended task. Jailbreaking tries to bypass safety restrictions. Attacks can overlap.Redirect a summarizer into advertising versus ask it to bypass prohibited-content safeguards.
Prompt-injection defencesDefensive prompts are one layer, not a complete security boundary. Combine them with restricted tools, authorization, input/output checks and treatment of retrieved text as untrusted data.A document cannot grant the assistant permission to delete files simply by containing an instruction.
Human bias versus algorithmic biasHuman choices can introduce bias; model outcomes can reflect historical data bias. These concepts overlap rather than forming perfectly exclusive categories.A scientist chooses features based on stereotypes; a trained hiring model then favours one gender.
Explainability benefitsHelps users understand results, builds informed trust, and assists debugging. Concealing model logic is not explainability.Discover that a loan prediction relied too heavily on an inappropriate feature.
Service roleAn IAM role assumed by an AWS service. Its trust policy determines who may assume it; permissions determine allowed actions.Bedrock reads only an approved S3 prefix through its service role.
Team isolation for RAGRestrict the service role actually reading data, plus application authorization, knowledge-base access and retrieval boundaries. A user's narrow S3 role does not automatically restrict a broader service role.Team A can query only its authorized client collection, with matching storage and retrieval permissions.
Least privilege for peopleAssign roles according to job needs and use temporary credentials where appropriate. A separate role for every person is not universally required.Analysts share an approved read-only role; administrators receive separately controlled permissions.
AWS ArtifactProvides AWS and participating third-party compliance reports and agreements, with configurable notifications for available report updates.Receive notice of a new supplier SOC report and download it.
Config, Audit Manager and CloudTrailConfig checks resource configurations; Audit Manager collects audit evidence; CloudTrail records supported account/API activity. CloudTrail does not literally log every possible event automatically.Check a bucket rule; assemble audit evidence; identify who changed a policy.
Inspector versus Trusted AdvisorInspector identifies supported software vulnerabilities and exposure findings. Trusted Advisor provides broader checks and recommendations.Find a vulnerable package versus review resource-optimization recommendations.
EC2 is IaaSRent compute infrastructure and choose an AMI/OS configuration. AWS manages underlying infrastructure; you manage the guest OS and applications.Launch Linux on an EC2 instance and install your application.
Cloud advantagesTrade upfront capital expense for variable expense, benefit from economies of scale, and deploy globally quickly.Rent capacity when needed rather than purchase a data centre.
Region, AZ and global servicesAn AWS Region has at least three AZs; an AZ has one or more discrete data centres. Lambda and Rekognition are regional; IAM and CloudFront are global in scope.Deploy a Lambda function in a chosen Region.
WAF scopeAWS WAF can protect regional resources or CloudFront distributions; its scope depends on the protected resource.Regional protection for an application load balancer; global scope for CloudFront.
Maximum security ownershipBuilding and training a model from scratch gives the customer the greatest scope of model/application responsibilities among the listed GenAI scenarios. AWS still manages its underlying physical infrastructure.Own data selection, training, deployment and model safeguards rather than just consume a hosted assistant.

Exam-focused coverage of all five published domains, with your original course tables retained. The AWS guide is non-exhaustive: no notes can list every possible exam question or guarantee a pass. The aim is to understand the choices and apply them to unfamiliar scenarios.

TopicSimple explanationExample / application

Generative AI24% of scored content. Tokens, architectures, capabilities, costs, context and agentsUse the matching domain in the scenario atlas and review the linked AWS objectives.

Responsible AI14% of scored content. Fairness, robustness, explainability, safety and human oversightUse the matching domain in the scenario atlas and review the linked AWS objectives.
Security & governance14% of scored content. Access, encryption, privacy, audits and governanceUse the matching domain in the scenario atlas and review the linked AWS objectives.

The certification focuses on conceptual understanding and business use cases. Detailed algorithm coding, implementation of feature engineering, mathematical analysis, and building production pipelines are not target job tasks. Learn what to choose and why, rather than implementation commands.

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
Format and score65 questions: 50 scored and 15 unidentified unscored. AWS reports a scaled score of 100–1000; 700 is the passing score. Raw practice percentages do not directly convert to this scale.Use practice scores to find weak topics rather than infer an exact AWS result.
Question typesSingle answer, multiple response, matching and ordering. Multiple-response and structured questions require the complete correct response for credit.For Select TWO, choose exactly both correct options; one correct choice is insufficient.
Timing90 minutes standard. A separately approved 30-minute accommodation gives 120 minutes.Use the appropriate timer in the website.
How to read a scenarioIdentify the required input, output, learning data, action, constraint and business objective before choosing a service.Recorded call → text: Transcribe. Scanned invoice → text: Textract. Existing text → sentiment: Comprehend.
No automatic certaintyA model name, large size, low temperature, citation or high average score does not by itself prove the answer is correct or the application safe.Check source support, subgroup results and actual task completion.
Conflicting practice keysSeparate a source key from a reliable rule. Ambiguous or outdated items should teach a distinction, not a false absolute.More epochs cannot be prescribed solely because accuracy is low; first inspect training and validation curves.
MCP, tools and authorizationMCP connects tools/context; it does not grant access. Tool execution must still satisfy application and resource policies.An agent discovers a refund tool, but a policy still limits who can invoke it.
AgentCore Identity versus PolicyIdentity concerns agent credentials and delegated access. Policy governs supported tool interactions at the enforcement boundary.Use identity to access a connected service and an action policy to restrict what can be done.
Agent evaluation layersCheck tool selection, tool inputs, intermediate results, final answers, completed actions and cost.A polite response is not success if the refund API failed.
RAG evaluation layersCheck retrieval relevance/coverage, evidence support, answer correctness and end-to-end user outcomes.An accurate model cannot answer from a missing policy passage; fix retrieval before blaming generation.
Global and local explanationsA global explanation summarizes broad model behaviour. A local explanation addresses a particular prediction; SHAP can support both local and aggregated views.A partial dependence plot shows average model response as a feature varies; a case-level attribution explains one prediction.
Predictive versus causal explanationFeature influence on a prediction does not by itself prove that changing the feature causes an outcome.A location feature affects a risk score; that does not establish a causal effect of moving home.
Class threshold trade-offChanging a classification threshold changes precision/recall and error counts. Select a threshold for business costs using validation data.Lower a fraud threshold to catch more cases, while assessing added false alarms.
Drift versus low initial qualityData drift concerns changed inputs; concept drift concerns changed input–outcome relationships. Neither is repaired just by increasing alert frequency.Customer behaviour changes after a new product launch; investigate and evaluate a suitable update.
Pseudonymization versus anonymizationPseudonymization replaces identifiers but may retain a reversible mapping. Anonymization aims to prevent identification; effectiveness depends on re-identification risk.Replace a customer name with a token and restrict the separate mapping.
Data lineage versus catalogLineage traces origins and transformations. A catalog describes available data and metadata.Trace a feature back to a source table versus find a table description.
Data retention versus residencyRetention is how long data is kept; residency is where it is stored or processed under the applicable requirement.Delete records after an approved period while keeping them in an approved Region.
Prompt caching versus answer cachingPrompt caching reuses supported processing of repeated input prefixes. Answer caching reuses a previously produced result and needs freshness/authorization controls.Reuse the same long instruction prefix while generating different replies.
Newer names and older course termsThe current guide lists Amazon Quick, Kiro, Strands Agents, AgentCore and AWS Transform. Older Q-related topics remain useful for interpreting your uploaded tests.Business work/insights → Quick; development → Kiro; agent SDK → Strands; modernization → Transform.
Availability and quotasCheck current regional/model support and service limits instead of treating old default choices or pricing claims as universal.A custom model may have supported on-demand deployment; Provisioned Throughput is inference capacity, not the training operation.

Scenario atlas — Domain 1: AI & machine learning

Transfer learning

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningAdapt knowledge learned on one task to a related task.Reuse a pretrained vision model when labelled specialist images are limited.
Common trapUpdating the same model with arriving data is incremental training, not necessarily transfer learning.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A factory adapts a pretrained general-image model using a small collection of labelled defective-part images. Which technique reuses the earlier learning?Knowledge from general images is reused for a related inspection task.
Example 2A hospital starts with a pretrained image encoder rather than randomly initialized weights and adapts it to a specialist image task. What is this approach?The starting knowledge comes from an already-trained model.
Example 3A sentiment model learned from product reviews is adapted to restaurant reviews. Which approach is being used?Knowledge transfers between related text-classification domains.
Example 4A team adapts a general speech model for recognising specialist technical vocabulary with labelled recordings. What learning approach is illustrated?Existing speech representations are reused for a related task.
Example 5A wildlife project has few labelled images and adapts an existing vision network. What reduces the need to learn visual features from scratch?Pretrained visual features are transferred to wildlife classification.
Example 6A developer initializes a document classifier from a model trained on another language task and then trains on labelled support tickets. Which technique is this?The new task benefits from previously learned language representations.
Compare: Incremental trainingUpdate an existing model with newly available data without necessarily restarting from scratch.Use it when: Refresh a same-task model using new labelled records.
Compare: K-means clusteringFind K groups of similar examples without target category labels.Use it when: Explore natural groups such as customer behaviour segments.
Compare: Reinforcement learningAn agent learns behaviour through interaction and reward feedback.Use it when: Train a simulated controller to maximize a reward over time.

Semi-supervised learning

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningUse labelled and unlabelled examples together in training.A small labelled collection is available alongside much more unlabelled data.
Common trapA business task name alone does not determine its learning type; inspect the training data and objective.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A team trains with 500 images labelled by experts and 20,000 unlabelled images, using both sets to improve a classifier. Which learning approach fits?Training combines labelled and unlabelled examples.
Example 2A bank uses confirmed fraud labels for a small subset of transactions and incorporates a large unlabelled transaction pool into training. Which approach is this?Both data types participate in the learning process.
Example 3Only 2% of customer reviews have sentiment labels. The training method also uses the remaining unlabelled reviews. Which method fits?The label shortage is addressed with unlabelled data as well as known answers.
Example 4A speech classifier learns from a few annotated clips and many unannotated clips. Which learning category best describes the mixed dataset approach?The approach mixes explicit labels with unlabelled examples.
Example 5A medical-text classifier uses clinician-labelled notes together with a larger set of notes without diagnostic labels. Which training approach fits?A partially labelled collection is used jointly.
Example 6A document team manually labels 1,000 contracts and trains using those plus 50,000 unlabelled contracts. Which approach describes this?The model uses a mixture of known labels and unlabelled data.
Compare: Self-supervised learningDerive prediction targets from the data itself.Use it when: Learn representations from large text or image collections without manual task labels.
Compare: Supervised learningLearn from examples with known target labels or numerical answers.Use it when: Train on transactions already labelled fraud or legitimate.
Compare: K-means clusteringFind K groups of similar examples without target category labels.Use it when: Explore natural groups such as customer behaviour segments.

Self-supervised learning

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningDerive prediction targets from the data itself.Learn representations from large text or image collections without manual task labels.
Common trapUnlabelled input does not mean there is no training target: the process constructs one.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A language model hides words in ordinary text and learns to recover them. No people supply word-by-word answer labels. Which approach is this?Hidden words provide targets derived from the original data.
Example 2A model learns to predict the next token from earlier tokens in a document corpus. Which approach creates its supervision from the text?The following token becomes the target automatically.
Example 3A vision model masks image patches and learns to reconstruct them from the rest of each image. Which training approach fits?The original image supplies the missing-patch targets.
Example 4A team builds paired training inputs and targets by removing parts of otherwise unlabelled sentences. Which approach is illustrated?The labels arise from a transformation of the data itself.
Example 5An encoder learns useful representations by comparing different augmented views of the same images, without category labels. Which approach best fits?Relationships constructed from the examples provide a self-supervised objective.
Example 6A foundation model trains on a large corpus by predicting withheld pieces of its own input. Which approach is most directly described?The prediction task supplies supervision without manual category annotations.
Compare: Semi-supervised learningUse labelled and unlabelled examples together in training.Use it when: A small labelled collection is available alongside much more unlabelled data.
Compare: Reinforcement learningAn agent learns behaviour through interaction and reward feedback.Use it when: Train a simulated controller to maximize a reward over time.
Compare: Supervised learningLearn from examples with known target labels or numerical answers.Use it when: Train on transactions already labelled fraud or legitimate.

K-means clustering

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningFind K groups of similar examples without target category labels.Explore natural groups such as customer behaviour segments.
Common trapK in K-means means cluster count; KNN uses K labelled neighbours.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A retailer has purchase histories but no segment labels. It wants exactly four behaviour groups. Which technique fits?K-means forms a chosen number of groups without supplied target labels.
Example 2A marketing team wants five clusters of similar customers using spending and visit frequency. Which approach fits?Similarity-based grouping with K=5 is clustering.
Example 3An analyst explores three natural groups of stores based on sales profiles without known categories. Which algorithm fits?There are no known output labels and three clusters are desired.
Example 4A company groups unlabeled sensor readings into six operating-pattern clusters. Which method fits?K specifies the number of similarity groups.
Example 5A website groups visitors into four segments before naming the segments. Which approach fits?Group discovery occurs before any category names are assigned.
Example 6A travel company asks for seven groups of destinations with similar numerical characteristics, without predefined group labels. Which technique fits?K-means partitions observations into seven clusters.
Compare: K-nearest neighboursUse nearby labelled examples to classify or predict a numerical target.Use it when: Classify a new item by the labels of its closest known neighbours.
Compare: RegressionPredict a numerical quantity from input features.Use it when: Estimate price, demand quantity or duration.
Compare: Association rule learningDiscover items or events that tend to occur together.Use it when: Find products often bought in the same basket.

Regression

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningPredict a numerical quantity from input features.Estimate price, demand quantity or duration.
Common trapNumbers used as category codes still represent classification; inspect what the output means.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A model predicts the sale price of a house in pounds. Which ML task fits?The desired output is a numerical amount, not a category.
Example 2A delivery model estimates the number of minutes until an order arrives. Which task fits?The output is a duration on a numerical scale.
Example 3A factory predicts the continuous strength of a material from its measurements. Which task fits?The target is a measured quantity.
Example 4A shop predicts next week's total revenue as a currency amount. Which type of prediction is this?Revenue is numerical rather than a class label.
Example 5A model estimates electricity consumption in kilowatt-hours. Which task best describes this?The output is a quantity with meaningful numerical differences.
Example 6A company predicts the expected repair cost of a damaged vehicle. Which learning task fits?A cost estimate is a numerical regression target.
Compare: ClassificationPredict a category from input features.Use it when: Predict spam/not spam or one of several product categories.
Compare: K-means clusteringFind K groups of similar examples without target category labels.Use it when: Explore natural groups such as customer behaviour segments.
Compare: Association rule learningDiscover items or events that tend to occur together.Use it when: Find products often bought in the same basket.

Recall

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningTP / (TP + FN): the fraction of actual positives detected.Prioritize finding actual positives when missed cases are costly.
Common trapPrecision asks how many alerts are correct; recall asks how many actual cases were caught.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A fraud team wants to measure the fraction of all actual fraud cases that its model catches. Which metric should it use?Actual fraud is the denominator; detected fraud is the numerator.
Example 2A screening model misses many actual positive cases. Which metric directly measures its ability to find those cases?Misses are false negatives, which reduce recall.
Example 3There are 80 actual fraudulent transactions and the model detects 60. Which metric is 75% here?Recall is 60 divided by 80.
Example 4A security team wants to minimize missed intrusions and asks which metric tracks the fraction of real intrusions detected. Which metric fits?Detection coverage of actual positives is recall.
Example 5A classifier flags only 20 of 100 actual defective products. Which metric equals 20%?It found 20 of the 100 actual positives.
Example 6A search evaluation asks how many of all relevant documents were retrieved. Which metric fits?Relevant retrieved documents divided by all relevant documents is recall.
Compare: PrecisionTP / (TP + FP): the fraction of predicted positives that are correct.Use it when: Reduce false alarms and measure alert reliability.
Compare: AccuracyThe fraction of all predictions that are correct, including both positive and negative classes.Use it when: Measure overall classification correctness when appropriate for the class distribution.
Compare: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)Square errors, average them and take the square root; larger errors receive greater weight.Use it when: Evaluate numerical regression predictions when large errors matter.

Precision

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningTP / (TP + FP): the fraction of predicted positives that are correct.Reduce false alarms and measure alert reliability.
Common trapA model can have perfect precision while missing most actual positives.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A bank wants to know what fraction of its fraud alerts correspond to actual fraud. Which metric fits?The denominator is all alerts, including false alarms.
Example 2A model creates 40 alerts, of which 30 are genuine fraud. Which metric equals 75%?Precision is 30 correct alerts out of 40 alerts.
Example 3Investigators are overloaded by legitimate transactions incorrectly flagged as fraud. Which metric directly measures alert quality?False positives reduce precision.
Example 4A search engine asks what proportion of retrieved documents is relevant. Which metric fits?The denominator is the retrieved set.
Example 5An inspection system marks 25 items defective, but only 20 are defective. Which metric is 80%?Precision is 20 divided by 25 flagged items.
Example 6A classifier has 90 true positives and 10 false positives. Which metric equals 90%?Precision uses TP divided by TP plus FP.
Compare: RecallTP / (TP + FN): the fraction of actual positives detected.Use it when: Prioritize finding actual positives when missed cases are costly.
Compare: AccuracyThe fraction of all predictions that are correct, including both positive and negative classes.Use it when: Measure overall classification correctness when appropriate for the class distribution.
Compare: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)Square errors, average them and take the square root; larger errors receive greater weight.Use it when: Evaluate numerical regression predictions when large errors matter.

Reduce overfitting

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningImprove generalization when training performance is strong but unseen-data performance is weak.Try suitable regularization, simpler models, representative data or early stopping.
Common trapPoor accuracy alone is insufficient evidence of overfitting. Compare training and validation.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1Training accuracy is 99%, but validation accuracy is 65%. Which approach best addresses the likely problem?The train-validation gap suggests memorization or excessive sensitivity.
Example 2Training loss keeps falling while validation loss starts rising. What should the team focus on?Worsening validation despite improving training is an overfitting signal.
Example 3A deep decision tree memorizes rare training cases and fails on new records. Which improvement goal fits?Reducing excessive complexity can improve generalization.
Example 4A model learns image-background quirks rather than robust object patterns and fails on new backgrounds. Which training concern should be addressed?Fragile training-specific patterns suggest overfitting.
Example 5A model is almost perfect on training examples but unstable on held-out examples from the same population. Which corrective focus fits?Training success is not transferring to unseen examples.
Example 6A team adds regularization after observing excellent training results and poor test results. What problem is it trying to reduce?Regularization is being used to limit an overly complex fit.
Compare: Reduce underfittingImprove a model that is too restrictive to learn useful patterns even on training data.Use it when: Consider richer features, more suitable complexity or less excessive regularization.
Compare: Increase training epochsTrain for additional complete passes through the dataset.Use it when: Consider when learning is incomplete and validation performance continues to improve; it can worsen overfitting.
Compare: Model inferenceUse an already-trained model to produce predictions or generated outputs.Use it when: Summarize a new email without updating model parameters.

Validation data

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningUse development-time held-out data to compare models and tune hyperparameters.Choose learning rates, thresholds and configurations before final testing.
Common trapRepeatedly tuning on the final test set contaminates the final evaluation.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A team compares five learning rates and selects the best before final evaluation. Which dataset should guide the selection?Hyperparameter selection is a development-time validation task.
Example 2Developers choose between a shallow and deep tree without looking at the reserved final test set. Which data should they use?Model choices should use validation data.
Example 3An engineer chooses an early-stopping point by checking performance after each epoch. Which dataset is appropriate?Repeated development decisions should be based on validation performance.
Example 4A team adjusts a classification threshold to balance precision and recall before a final independent assessment. Which dataset fits?Threshold tuning is part of model development.
Example 5A data scientist compares regularization strengths during model development. Which dataset should guide the choice?Validation evaluates candidate settings without using the final test set.
Example 6A project uses cross-validation folds to select settings. Which role do the held-out folds serve during this process?They serve the validation role for model selection.
Compare: Training dataExamples used to fit learned model parameters.Use it when: Learn weights from the training split.
Compare: Test dataProvide a final independent evaluation after model choices have been made.Use it when: Estimate final generalization without using those records for tuning.
Compare: Model inferenceUse an already-trained model to produce predictions or generated outputs.Use it when: Summarize a new email without updating model parameters.

Convolutional neural network (CNN)

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningLearn spatial features such as edges, textures and shapes.Image classification and visual feature extraction, including video frames.
Common trapRNNs model sequences; CNNs are not limited to single still images.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A company trains a neural network to classify defects in individual product photographs. Which architecture is a conventional strong fit?Spatial patterns in images are the key input structure.
Example 2A vision system learns local edges and textures to distinguish animal species in camera images. Which architecture fits?Convolutions learn local spatial features.
Example 3A traffic application extracts visual features separately from every video frame. Which architecture can handle this spatial stage?CNNs can process each frame even when the overall input is video.
Example 4A project identifies handwritten digits from pixel arrays using local image filters. Which architecture is being described?Learned convolution filters detect spatial image patterns.
Example 5A factory needs image features representing cracks and surface scratches. Which architecture is best aligned with those patterns?Surface defects are spatial visual features.
Example 6A model applies learned convolution filters across images to detect product shapes. Which architecture fits?Convolution filters are characteristic of CNNs.
Compare: Recurrent neural network (RNN)Model sequences using a state carried between steps.Use it when: Learn patterns across time-series values, text or other sequences.
Compare: Generative adversarial networks (GANs)Train a generator and discriminator with competing objectives.Use it when: Synthesize realistic examples such as images or tabular records.
Compare: K-means clusteringFind K groups of similar examples without target category labels.Use it when: Explore natural groups such as customer behaviour segments.

SageMaker Feature Store

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningStore, manage and reuse ML features for training and inference.Share consistent features across teams and prediction workflows.
Common trapData Wrangler prepares data; Feature Store manages reusable features.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1Two teams need to share the same customer-spending features for training and online predictions. Which SageMaker capability fits?The requirement is centralized reuse of features.
Example 2A company wants a managed repository for engineered inputs used by several models. Which capability fits?Reusable engineered inputs are features.
Example 3Training and inference should use consistent definitions of customer transaction counts. Which SageMaker feature helps manage this?Feature Store supports shared feature values and definitions across workflows.
Example 4A team has already cleaned its data and now needs to store reusable model input features. Which capability fits?Preparation is finished; the requirement is feature storage.
Example 5Several fraud models need access to managed historical and current customer features. Which SageMaker capability fits?A feature repository supports training and serving use cases.
Example 6A data science group wants to discover and reuse existing features instead of recomputing them independently. Which service capability fits?Central feature management supports reuse and collaboration.
Compare: SageMaker Data WranglerExplore, visualize and transform data for ML workflows.Use it when: Clean data, create features and export a preparation flow.
Compare: SageMaker Ground TruthSupport human-in-the-loop work including creation of labelled training datasets.Use it when: Label training images and assess annotation quality.
Compare: SageMaker ClarifyAssess bias and explain model predictions with supported analysis tools.Use it when: Investigate feature influence and bias in data or model outcomes.

SageMaker Batch Transform

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningRun offline predictions for a stored dataset without maintaining a real-time endpoint.Large scheduled datasets where immediate responses are unnecessary.
Common trapBatch execution is asynchronous, but it is distinct from the named Async Inference endpoint option.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A retailer scores a 20-GB dataset in S3 overnight and does not need individual immediate responses. Which SageMaker inference option fits?This is offline inference over a large stored dataset.
Example 2A bank generates a complete monthly risk report from stored records. Which deployment option avoids a persistent online endpoint?The work is a scheduled batch rather than interactive traffic.
Example 3A company has millions of archived examples and wants one prediction file when processing finishes. Which option fits?Batch Transform processes stored datasets and writes results later.
Example 4A team runs predictions once each weekend over all warehouse records. Which SageMaker option best matches the workload?No real-time request-serving endpoint is needed.
Example 5A project processes a multi-gigabyte input dataset split across S3 objects for a nightly job. Which inference option is suitable?Dataset-scale offline processing is a batch use case.
Example 6A company requires predictions for its entire product catalogue before tomorrow morning. Which SageMaker approach fits?Deferred predictions for the full stored catalogue fit Batch Transform.
Compare: SageMaker Asynchronous InferenceQueue individual inference requests and return results later; supports up to 1-GB payloads and one-hour processing.Use it when: Serve large or long-running individual requests with deferred responses.
Compare: SageMaker Real-Time InferenceServe low-latency synchronous predictions through a persistent endpoint.Use it when: Provide interactive predictions with prompt request-response behaviour.
Compare: SageMaker Serverless InferenceServe supported intermittent workloads without provisioning serving instances; account for cold starts and limitations.Use it when: Handle sporadic suitable traffic that can tolerate cold starts.

SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningSearch hyperparameter configurations against a defined objective metric.Try learning rates or regularization settings to find a better configuration.
Common trapMLflow records experiments; AMT searches settings. Autotune can choose several search settings automatically.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A team wants SageMaker to try different learning rates and choose a configuration using validation performance. Which capability fits?The task is automated hyperparameter search.
Example 2Developers want to optimize regularization strength across several training jobs. Which SageMaker capability fits?Training settings must be searched against an objective.
Example 3A data scientist defines an objective metric and asks a service to search model hyperparameter combinations. Which service feature fits?AMT evaluates candidate configurations through training jobs.
Example 4A team needs to compare training settings automatically, rather than simply log previously completed runs. Which SageMaker capability fits?The key action is searching settings, not tracking them.
Example 5A model developer uses Autotune to help configure a hyperparameter search. Which SageMaker capability is being configured?Autotune assists Automatic Model Tuning.
Example 6A project wants a systematic search for a useful learning-rate and batch-size combination. Which SageMaker capability fits?These are hyperparameters varied across training configurations.
Compare: MLflow on SageMakerTrack ML experiments, parameters, metrics and artifacts.Use it when: Compare recorded training runs and reproduce experiments.
Compare: SageMaker Model RegistryManage model versions and associated lifecycle/approval information.Use it when: Track which model version is approved for deployment.
Compare: SageMaker Model MonitorMonitor deployed-model data and quality signals with supported monitoring types.Use it when: Detect drift or deterioration after deployment.

Official scope: AWS domain 1 objectives.

Scenario atlas — Domain 2: Generative AI

Tokens

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningUnits of text a model processes; a token may be a word, part of a word, or punctuation.Measure input/output length and many text-model inference charges.
Common trapOne word is not always one token.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A long technical word is split into several pieces before an LLM processes it. What are those pieces called?Tokenization creates model-readable text units.
Example 2A provider charges per thousand input and output text units. What units commonly underpin text-model pricing?Text-model usage is commonly metered in tokens.
Example 3An application counts subwords and punctuation sent to a model. What is it measuring?Those units are tokens, not necessarily whole words.
Example 4A chatbot generates its answer one model-readable text unit at a time. What is that unit?Autoregressive text generation predicts tokens.
Example 5A prompt contains 100 words but its measured model length is 145 units. What explains the different unit count?Words can be split into multiple tokens.
Example 6A team reduces repetitive text in a prompt to reduce input usage charges. Which units is it primarily reducing?Shorter prompt text usually reduces input tokens.
Compare: Context windowThe model-supported token budget for information considered in a request, with exact input/output accounting depending on the model.Use it when: Check whether instructions, history, retrieved text and response budget fit.
Compare: EmbeddingsNumerical vector representations used to compare meaning or other learned similarity.Use it when: Semantic search and matching related text or images.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.

Context window

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningThe model-supported token budget for information considered in a request, with exact input/output accounting depending on the model.Check whether instructions, history, retrieved text and response budget fit.
Common trapIncreasing maximum output tokens does not make an oversized input fit.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1Instructions, conversation history and a long document exceed the model's supported request length. Which limit is involved?The combined context must fit the model's window.
Example 2A chatbot cannot consider its entire conversation history at once. Which model property constrains this?Context capacity limits information available in a request.
Example 3A team chooses a model to analyse lengthy documents and checks how much text it can consider. Which property matters?Document length must fit the supported context window.
Example 4A developer increases output length but an oversized input is still rejected. Which limit remains the issue?Output limits do not expand the context window.
Example 5A RAG application must budget space for system instructions, retrieved passages and an answer. What model limit guides this budget?All context components compete for supported capacity.
Example 6An assistant must summarize older conversation turns to leave room for new information. Which constraint motivates this?Its context window is finite.
Compare: TokensUnits of text a model processes; a token may be a word, part of a word, or punctuation.Use it when: Measure input/output length and many text-model inference charges.
Compare: Maximum output tokensCap the number of tokens generated in a response.Use it when: Bound answer length and limit potential output usage.
Compare: EmbeddingsNumerical vector representations used to compare meaning or other learned similarity.Use it when: Semantic search and matching related text or images.

Embeddings

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningNumerical vector representations used to compare meaning or other learned similarity.Semantic search and matching related text or images.
Common trapAn embedding model produces vectors, not a complete conversational answer by itself.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A search system converts “refund” and “money back” into representations that can be compared for semantic similarity. What does it create?Learned vectors represent related meaning.
Example 2A multimodal search system maps product photos and descriptions into a compatible numerical space. What outputs support this matching?Multimodal embeddings support similarity comparisons across inputs.
Example 3A document application needs numerical representations for nearest-neighbour retrieval. What should it generate?Retrieval compares embedding vectors.
Example 4A customer asks a question using different words from a manual. Which representation helps find a semantically similar passage?Embeddings can match meaning without exact keyword equality.
Example 5An image search system stores learned vectors describing images for similarity lookup. What are these representations called?Embeddings encode useful characteristics numerically.
Example 6A company compares vector distances to identify related support tickets. What kind of representations is it comparing?Semantic embeddings support similarity search.
Compare: TokensUnits of text a model processes; a token may be a word, part of a word, or punctuation.Use it when: Measure input/output length and many text-model inference charges.
Compare: Diffusion modelsGenerate data by learning to reverse a noise-adding process, often refining noise into an image.Use it when: Text-guided image synthesis and other generative tasks.
Compare: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)Retrieve relevant external evidence and give it to a model as context for generation.Use it when: Frequently changing knowledge and answers grounded in approved documents.

Diffusion models

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningGenerate data by learning to reverse a noise-adding process, often refining noise into an image.Text-guided image synthesis and other generative tasks.
Common trapTwo competing networks describes a GAN, not diffusion.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1An image generator starts with noise and repeatedly denoises it according to a text description. Which model family fits?Iterative denoising characterizes diffusion.
Example 2A team trains a generator to reverse gradual corruption of images by noise. Which approach is described?Learning the reverse noise process is diffusion modelling.
Example 3A system progressively refines a noisy image sample into a realistic product illustration. Which model family fits?The generation process repeatedly removes noise.
Example 4A researcher compares a denoising-based generator with a generator-discriminator pair. What is the denoising family called?The competing pair is a GAN; denoising describes diffusion.
Example 5A text-to-image model learns noise-prediction steps and uses them to synthesize an image. Which family fits?Noise prediction supports the reverse diffusion process.
Example 6A generative model uses multiple denoising steps rather than an adversarial discriminator to create artwork. Which family fits?The described iterative reverse process is diffusion.
Compare: Generative adversarial networks (GANs)Train a generator and discriminator with competing objectives.Use it when: Synthesize realistic examples such as images or tabular records.
Compare: Transformer self-attentionRelate tokens to relevant context to form context-sensitive representations.Use it when: Language understanding and generation, with transformer variants supporting other modalities.
Compare: Convolutional neural network (CNN)Learn spatial features such as edges, textures and shapes.Use it when: Image classification and visual feature extraction, including video frames.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs)

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningTrain a generator and discriminator with competing objectives.Synthesize realistic examples such as images or tabular records.
Common trapSynthetic outputs are not automatically private or unbiased.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1One network makes artificial images while another tries to distinguish them from real images. Which architecture is this?A generator and discriminator compete.
Example 2A lab trains a data generator to fool a discriminator. Which model family fits?Adversarial training is the defining clue.
Example 3A project synthesizes records through a generator evaluated by a real-versus-generated classifier. What architecture is described?The classifier serves as a discriminator.
Example 4A researcher uses two competing networks for image synthesis rather than iterative denoising. Which family fits?Competing generator and discriminator networks indicate a GAN.
Example 5A model's training alternates between improving fake samples and improving detection of those samples. Which architecture fits?The two adversarial objectives define a GAN.
Example 6An image-generation project has components explicitly named generator and discriminator. Which architecture is it using?These are the characteristic GAN components.
Compare: Diffusion modelsGenerate data by learning to reverse a noise-adding process, often refining noise into an image.Use it when: Text-guided image synthesis and other generative tasks.
Compare: Convolutional neural network (CNN)Learn spatial features such as edges, textures and shapes.Use it when: Image classification and visual feature extraction, including video frames.
Compare: Transformer self-attentionRelate tokens to relevant context to form context-sensitive representations.Use it when: Language understanding and generation, with transformer variants supporting other modalities.

Transformer self-attention

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningRelate tokens to relevant context to form context-sensitive representations.Language understanding and generation, with transformer variants supporting other modalities.

Example 2An LLM relates each token to relevant tokens elsewhere in its context. Which mechanism is central to its Transformer architecture?Self-attention models contextual relationships.
Example 3A team describes an architecture using attention rather than a recurrent hidden-state sequence. Which model family fits?Attention is the distinguishing Transformer mechanism.
Example 4A summarizer needs to relate a pronoun to an earlier name using contextual token representations. Which architecture is well known for self-attention?Transformers use attention to connect relevant context.
Example 5A masked-language model such as BERT attends to context on both sides of a word. Which architecture underlies it?BERT is a bidirectional Transformer.
Example 6A model uses attention layers to build contextual embeddings rather than fixed meanings for every occurrence of a word. Which architecture fits?Contextual self-attention is the Transformer clue.
Compare: Generative adversarial networks (GANs)Train a generator and discriminator with competing objectives.Use it when: Synthesize realistic examples such as images or tabular records.
Compare: Diffusion modelsGenerate data by learning to reverse a noise-adding process, often refining noise into an image.Use it when: Text-guided image synthesis and other generative tasks.
Compare: Recurrent neural network (RNN)Model sequences using a state carried between steps.Use it when: Learn patterns across time-series values, text or other sequences.

Example 3An assistant must discover tool interfaces supplied by another system using a standard AI integration protocol. Which concept fits?MCP describes tool and context integration.
