Example 5An AI client connects to a server offering resources and callable tools using MCP. What does MCP primarily enable?It connects the AI application to external capabilities and context.
Example 6A project adopts a common client-server interface for agent tools but still separately configures IAM permissions. Which protocol is this?MCP integrates tools while authorization remains a separate concern.
Compare: Agent memoryRetain useful session or longer-lived information to support later interactions.Use it when: Remember relevant preferences or earlier task state under appropriate privacy controls.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.
Compare: EmbeddingsNumerical vector representations used to compare meaning or other learned similarity.Use it when: Semantic search and matching related text or images.

Agent memory

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningRetain useful session or longer-lived information to support later interactions.Remember relevant preferences or earlier task state under appropriate privacy controls.
Common trapMemory is not the same as updating model weights.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1An assistant should remember a user's approved travel preference across sessions without retraining its model. Which capability fits?External memory can retain preferences without weight changes.
Example 2A multi-step assistant records completed steps so it can resume a task. Which capability supports this?Task state is retained in memory.
Example 3An agent recalls a previous conversation's relevant context from a managed store. Which concept is involved?The information is retrieved from memory rather than learned through training.
Example 4A team separates short-lived conversation state from longer-lived user preferences. Which agent design area is this?These are short-term and long-term memory concerns.
Example 5An assistant must carry forward an approved delivery preference into a later interaction. Which capability helps?Persistent contextual information can be stored as memory.
Example 6A project lets users delete remembered preferences independently of the base model. Which capability is being managed?External agent memory can be governed independently of model weights.
Compare: Supervised fine-tuningUpdate pretrained model weights using task-specific input–output examples.Use it when: Teach consistent task behaviour or style when prompting alone is inadequate and good training examples exist.
Compare: EmbeddingsNumerical vector representations used to compare meaning or other learned similarity.Use it when: Semantic search and matching related text or images.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.

Context engineering

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningSelect and organize the instructions, retrieved data, history, memory and tool results supplied to a model.Provide useful context within length, cost and privacy constraints.
Common trapIt is broader than editing one instruction sentence and does not require model training.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1An application chooses relevant history, retrieved passages and tool results to fit into a prompt budget. What practice is this?It is engineering the complete context supplied to the model.
Example 2A team removes irrelevant retrieved passages and adds the latest tool result before generation. Which practice improves the information supplied to the model?Context engineering selects and structures useful information.
Example 3An assistant summarizes older history while preserving instructions and recent evidence. Which practice is this?The goal is effective context use within a finite window.
Example 4A developer coordinates system instructions, memory and retrieval content for every request. What is this called?Context engineering manages multiple context sources.
Example 5A RAG system decides what information to include, in what order, and how much space each source receives. Which practice fits?The task is context construction rather than parameter training.
Example 6A company removes unauthorized documents before assembling the model's prompt and includes only relevant evidence. Which broader design practice is involved?Secure selection of input context is part of context engineering.
Compare: Supervised fine-tuningUpdate pretrained model weights using task-specific input–output examples.Use it when: Teach consistent task behaviour or style when prompting alone is inadequate and good training examples exist.
Compare: Model distillationTrain a student model using outputs or guidance from a teacher model.Use it when: Seek a smaller or cheaper model that approximates useful teacher behaviour.
Compare: Increase training epochsTrain for additional complete passes through the dataset.Use it when: Consider when learning is incomplete and validation performance continues to improve; it can worsen overfitting.

Agent workflow orchestration

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningCoordinate task steps, tools or specialist agents and manage their handoffs.Multi-step work with dependencies, checks and controlled actions.
Common trapMore agents do not automatically produce better answers; coordination adds cost and failure modes.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A supervisor agent assigns research to one specialist and verification to another, then combines their results. What is the main pattern?The workflow coordinates specialist agents and handoffs.
Example 2A system must retrieve an order, check eligibility, request approval and then call a refund API. What organizes these dependent steps?Orchestration controls the task sequence and actions.
Example 3Several agents work on separate parts of a report before a coordinator consolidates outputs. Which concept fits?Multi-agent orchestration coordinates parallel work and aggregation.
Example 4An assistant handles tool failures with retries and routes a task to a human when a prerequisite fails. Which design area fits?Workflow orchestration manages branching and failures.
Example 5A business task needs an agent to call tools in a defined dependency order. What capability is most directly needed?Orchestration connects dependent tool steps.
Example 6A team defines which specialist handles each stage and how results are passed between agents. Which practice fits?It defines agent communication and workflow coordination.
Compare: EmbeddingsNumerical vector representations used to compare meaning or other learned similarity.Use it when: Semantic search and matching related text or images.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.
Compare: Model distillationTrain a student model using outputs or guidance from a teacher model.Use it when: Seek a smaller or cheaper model that approximates useful teacher behaviour.

Latency

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningElapsed time to obtain a response, often measured per request or at a percentile.Evaluate responsiveness for interactive applications.
Common trapThroughput measures completed work per unit time; accuracy measures correctness.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A trading application must return a prediction quickly after each request. Which metric most directly evaluates this requirement?Time per response is latency.
Example 2A voice assistant feels slow even though its answers are correct. Which metric should the team inspect first?The concern is response delay rather than answer quality.
Example 3A team measures the average number of milliseconds between request submission and response. What metric is this?Milliseconds per response measure latency.
Example 4A chatbot must satisfy a p95 response-time requirement. Which runtime metric is constrained?p95 latency describes the slower end of response times.
Example 5A customer-facing model produces only a few requests per minute but must answer each immediately. Which metric matters most here?Low request volume does not remove the response-time requirement.
Example 6A business compares two equally accurate models and prefers the one that answers sooner. Which metric drives the choice?Faster individual responses mean lower latency.
Compare: ThroughputThe amount of work completed per unit time.Use it when: Measure requests per second or documents processed per hour.
Compare: AccuracyThe fraction of all predictions that are correct, including both positive and negative classes.Use it when: Measure overall classification correctness when appropriate for the class distribution.
Compare: PrecisionTP / (TP + FP): the fraction of predicted positives that are correct.Use it when: Reduce false alarms and measure alert reliability.

On-demand inference pricing

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningPay for actual supported model usage without reserving sustained model capacity.Variable or experimental usage where a capacity commitment is undesirable.
Common trapProvisioned Throughput reserves capacity; pricing depends on the model and modality.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A startup cannot predict its request volume and wants to avoid reserved-capacity commitments. Which pricing approach fits?Usage-based on-demand access matches uncertain demand.
Example 2A team experiments with a supported model a few times each day and does not need reserved throughput. Which option fits?Sporadic experiments do not justify sustained reserved capacity.
Example 3A company wants to pay for the actual input and output usage of a supported model as requests arrive. Which pricing mode fits?On-demand pricing meters actual usage.
Example 4An application is in a pilot stage with unpredictable traffic. Which approach avoids committing to dedicated model capacity?On-demand suits uncertain pilot usage.
Example 5Developers try several supported FMs before choosing one and want flexible pay-per-use access. Which option fits?They need usage-based access rather than reserved throughput.
Example 6A small chatbot has occasional traffic and no guaranteed-capacity requirement. Which pricing approach is the natural starting point?On-demand avoids reserving unnecessary sustained capacity.
Compare: Provisioned ThroughputReserve model capacity under supported service arrangements.Use it when: Plan predictable sustained throughput when justified by workload and pricing.
Compare: SageMaker Batch TransformRun offline predictions for a stored dataset without maintaining a real-time endpoint.Use it when: Large scheduled datasets where immediate responses are unnecessary.
Compare: Supervised fine-tuningUpdate pretrained model weights using task-specific input–output examples.Use it when: Teach consistent task behaviour or style when prompting alone is inadequate and good training examples exist.

Model distillation

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningTrain a student model using outputs or guidance from a teacher model.Seek a smaller or cheaper model that approximates useful teacher behaviour.
Common trapThe student changes weights; it need not outperform the teacher or reproduce all capabilities.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A large model generates examples used to train a smaller student for cheaper inference. Which technique fits?A teacher guides student training.
Example 2A company wants a compact model to approximate a larger model's answers for one task. Which approach fits?Distillation transfers selected behaviour into a student.
Example 3During training, a student learns from a teacher model's output distributions. Which technique is this?Teacher-generated supervision is the distillation clue.
Example 4A team spends more during preparation to train a smaller model with a larger model's responses, aiming to reduce serving costs. What approach is this?Upfront teacher-guided training can lower later inference costs.
Example 5A deployed student no longer calls its teacher for every request after teacher-guided training. Which technique produced it?Distillation trains the student before independent inference.
Example 6A model-compression project uses a powerful model as a teacher rather than just retrieving documents at runtime. Which technique fits?The student learns model behaviour through training.
Compare: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)Retrieve relevant external evidence and give it to a model as context for generation.Use it when: Frequently changing knowledge and answers grounded in approved documents.
Compare: Supervised fine-tuningUpdate pretrained model weights using task-specific input–output examples.Use it when: Teach consistent task behaviour or style when prompting alone is inadequate and good training examples exist.

Scenario atlas — Domain 3: Foundation-model applications

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningRetrieve relevant external evidence and give it to a model as context for generation.Frequently changing knowledge and answers grounded in approved documents.
Common trapUpdate and synchronize the source/index; RAG reduces but does not eliminate hallucinations.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A refund policy changes weekly. A chatbot must answer from the latest approved policy without retraining its weights. Which approach fits?Retrieve current policy passages at inference time.
Example 2A law firm wants answers grounded in its private document collection with source references. Which approach fits?External documents supply evidence for generated answers.
Example 3A company needs a chatbot to use new product manuals as soon as their search index is updated. Which approach fits?Runtime retrieval supplies knowledge without a weight update.
Example 4An assistant should consult authoritative HR documents before answering employee questions. Which technique fits?It retrieves supporting information for the answer.
Example 5A model lacks private company facts that must remain independently updateable. Which approach supplies those facts during inference?RAG keeps source knowledge outside model weights.
Example 6A support tool finds the relevant troubleshooting passages and includes them in the model prompt. Which technique is being used?Retrieval followed by grounded generation is RAG.
Compare: Supervised fine-tuningUpdate pretrained model weights using task-specific input–output examples.Use it when: Teach consistent task behaviour or style when prompting alone is inadequate and good training examples exist.
Compare: Continued pre-trainingContinue training a pretrained model on an additional domain corpus, often using self-supervised objectives.Use it when: Adapt to domain language and patterns using substantial unlabelled text.
Compare: Model distillationTrain a student model using outputs or guidance from a teacher model.Use it when: Seek a smaller or cheaper model that approximates useful teacher behaviour.

Supervised fine-tuning

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningUpdate pretrained model weights using task-specific input–output examples.Teach consistent task behaviour or style when prompting alone is inadequate and good training examples exist.
Common trapFew-shot examples in a prompt do not change weights; RAG is better for frequently changing facts.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1After evaluating prompts, a company trains its model on thousands of approved question-answer examples to improve a specialist task. Which method is this?Labelled examples are used to update weights.
Example 2A team updates a pretrained model using pairs of customer requests and ideal brand-style replies. Which approach fits?Supervised input-output training teaches the desired behaviour.
Example 3An organization has a curated labelled dataset and wants its supported FM to learn a repeated output format through training. What method fits?Weight-changing training with target outputs is supervised fine-tuning.
Example 4A specialist classifier adapts a pretrained language model using annotated examples. Which method is described?Labels supervise parameter updates.
Example 5A team decides prompting is insufficient and trains on approved instruction-and-response pairs. Which customization approach fits?The examples become training data rather than inference context.
Example 6A company creates a private customized model by training on labelled task examples. Which technique changes its learned parameters?Supervised fine-tuning updates weights using known target responses.
Compare: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)Retrieve relevant external evidence and give it to a model as context for generation.Use it when: Frequently changing knowledge and answers grounded in approved documents.
Compare: Few-shot promptingInclude a few task examples in the inference prompt.Use it when: Show an output pattern without training or changing model weights.
Compare: Continued pre-trainingContinue training a pretrained model on an additional domain corpus, often using self-supervised objectives.Use it when: Adapt to domain language and patterns using substantial unlabelled text.

Continued pre-training

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningContinue training a pretrained model on an additional domain corpus, often using self-supervised objectives.Adapt to domain language and patterns using substantial unlabelled text.
Common trapTraining is not a reliable way to keep rapidly changing facts current.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A model continues training on a large unlabelled collection of engineering documents to learn domain language. Which approach fits?The additional corpus supports continued pre-training.
Example 2A biotechnology team trains an existing FM further on unlabelled scientific text. Which customization method is described?It continues domain-corpus training rather than using labelled response pairs.
Example 3A company wants an FM to learn specialist terminology through further self-supervised training. Which method fits?The objective and unlabelled corpus indicate continued pre-training.
Example 4A publisher has a large curated text corpus but no task-specific question-answer labels and wants domain adaptation through training. Which approach fits?Further corpus training can adapt domain representations.
Example 5A team resumes pretraining of an existing model using new domain text. What is this process called?It extends the pretraining process instead of starting from scratch.
Example 6A supported model is further trained to predict tokens in a proprietary unlabelled technical corpus. Which approach fits?Token-prediction training on new domain text is continued pre-training.
Compare: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)Retrieve relevant external evidence and give it to a model as context for generation.Use it when: Frequently changing knowledge and answers grounded in approved documents.
Compare: Few-shot promptingInclude a few task examples in the inference prompt.Use it when: Show an output pattern without training or changing model weights.
Compare: Model distillationTrain a student model using outputs or guidance from a teacher model.Use it when: Seek a smaller or cheaper model that approximates useful teacher behaviour.

Few-shot prompting

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningInclude a few task examples in the inference prompt.Show an output pattern without training or changing model weights.
Common trapFew-shot works with pretrained models; it does not require a new untrained model.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A prompt includes three input-and-output examples before asking a pretrained model to process a new input. Which technique is this?Examples are provided within the prompt.
Example 2A developer adds two examples of correct JSON responses without running training. Which technique fits?In-context demonstrations guide the output format.
Example 3A chatbot prompt shows several customer messages paired with their intents, then asks for the next intent. Which technique is used?Demonstrations precede the new task inside one context.
Example 4An analyst shows a model four correctly formatted summaries before supplying a new document. Which technique fits?A small set of examples guides inference.
Example 5A company improves reply tone by adding sample replies to the prompt and leaving model weights unchanged. Which approach is this?Examples in context are few-shot prompting.
Example 6A pretrained model receives two worked classification examples and one new item to classify. Which technique best describes the setup?The task uses a few demonstrations rather than a training update.
Compare: Supervised fine-tuningUpdate pretrained model weights using task-specific input–output examples.Use it when: Teach consistent task behaviour or style when prompting alone is inadequate and good training examples exist.
Compare: Continued pre-trainingContinue training a pretrained model on an additional domain corpus, often using self-supervised objectives.Use it when: Adapt to domain language and patterns using substantial unlabelled text.
Compare: Zero-shot promptingAsk a model to do a task without including worked examples.Use it when: Give a clear instruction to classify a new message with no demonstrations.

Temperature

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.
Common trapTemperature is not latency, a factuality guarantee, or a substitute for tone instructions.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A writer wants more varied wording across repeated responses to the same prompt. Which parameter most directly controls sampling randomness?Temperature changes the sampling distribution's randomness.
Example 2A team wants more predictable wording while keeping the model and prompt fixed. Which parameter would it typically lower?Lower temperature commonly reduces variation.
Example 3An application intentionally increases creative variation among candidate slogans. Which parameter is most relevant?Temperature is the primary randomness control.
Example 4A model tends to choose lower-probability continuations more often after a sampling adjustment. Which parameter was likely increased?Higher temperature typically spreads probability more broadly.
Example 5A developer wants to tune randomness rather than the number of candidate tokens. Which parameter fits?Temperature affects sampling sharpness, not a fixed candidate count.
Example 6A support team lowers one inference setting to reduce wording variation but still checks facts separately. Which setting is it lowering?Lower temperature improves predictability without proving accuracy.
Compare: Top KKeep a fixed count of highest-probability next-token candidates before sampling.Use it when: Limit the candidate pool by number.
Compare: Top PKeep a high-probability candidate set based on cumulative probability mass.Use it when: Use nucleus sampling with a probability threshold.
Compare: Maximum output tokensCap the number of tokens generated in a response.Use it when: Bound answer length and limit potential output usage.

Top K

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningKeep a fixed count of highest-probability next-token candidates before sampling.Limit the candidate pool by number.
Common trapThe model chooses a next token from the pool; it does not output all K candidates.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A developer wants to limit next-token sampling to the five most likely candidates. Which parameter fits?The restriction is a fixed candidate count.
Example 2An LLM is configured to consider only its three highest-probability next tokens. Which setting specifies three?K counts candidates.
Example 3A team chooses a sampling limit based on number of candidates rather than cumulative probability. Which parameter fits?Top K uses a count.
Example 4A generation configuration keeps the ten most likely token choices at each step. Which parameter is described?A top-ten candidate pool is Top K.
Example 5Dog, cat and horse are the three most likely next tokens. A setting keeps exactly those three as candidates. Which setting is it?Top K=3 keeps the highest-ranked three candidates.
Example 6An engineer changes a candidate-count setting from 20 to 5. Which inference parameter is being adjusted?The parameter controls how many top-ranked tokens remain eligible.
Compare: Top PKeep a high-probability candidate set based on cumulative probability mass.Use it when: Use nucleus sampling with a probability threshold.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.
Compare: Maximum output tokensCap the number of tokens generated in a response.Use it when: Bound answer length and limit potential output usage.

Top P

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningKeep a high-probability candidate set based on cumulative probability mass.Use nucleus sampling with a probability threshold.
Common trapP is not the percentage of vocabulary tokens. Candidate count varies with the distribution.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A sampler keeps the smallest leading token set whose combined probability reaches 0.9. Which setting is this?The threshold applies to cumulative probability.
Example 2A team uses nucleus sampling rather than a fixed candidate count. Which parameter fits?Top P defines the probability-mass nucleus.
Example 3Token probabilities are 50%, 20%, 12%, 10% and 8%. A threshold of 0.75 keeps the first three. Which parameter controls this?Their cumulative probability reaches 82%, crossing 75%.
Example 4A model includes more or fewer candidates depending on how concentrated their probabilities are. The target is a cumulative threshold. Which setting fits?Top P adapts candidate count to probability mass.
Example 5A developer wants to consider a high-probability set totaling at least 95% before sampling. Which parameter fits?Cumulative probability, rather than a fixed K, is specified.
Example 6A team adjusts a nucleus threshold from 0.9 to 0.7. Which inference parameter is it changing?The nucleus threshold is Top P.
Compare: Top KKeep a fixed count of highest-probability next-token candidates before sampling.Use it when: Limit the candidate pool by number.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.
Compare: Maximum output tokensCap the number of tokens generated in a response.Use it when: Bound answer length and limit potential output usage.

Maximum output tokens

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningCap the number of tokens generated in a response.Bound answer length and limit potential output usage.
Common trapA cap is not an exact word count and does not expand the context window.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A developer wants a hard upper token limit on generated responses. Which setting fits?Maximum output tokens caps generation length.
Example 2A chatbot should generate at most 200 tokens per reply. Which setting should be configured?The requirement is an upper output-token bound.
Example 3A company wants to limit the maximum amount of generated text for cost control. Which setting fits?The output-token cap limits possible generation volume.
Example 4A model should stop after a token budget even if it could continue. Which setting implements that limit?Maximum output tokens bounds the length.
Example 5An application allocates a 500-token response budget separately from its input. Which parameter represents that budget?It is the maximum generated-token setting.
Example 6A team needs shorter replies and chooses a maximum token allowance rather than a stop phrase. Which parameter is being set?Output length is being bounded numerically.
Compare: Stop sequenceEnd generation when a specified text sequence is produced, subject to model support.Use it when: Stop output at an agreed delimiter such as END.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.
Compare: Top KKeep a fixed count of highest-probability next-token candidates before sampling.Use it when: Limit the candidate pool by number.

AI agent with tools

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningUse a model to help plan and perform steps through authorized tools or APIs.Tasks require actions, such as checking eligibility and submitting a request.
Common trapA generated statement that an action happened is not proof; verify the tool result.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A support assistant must check an order, verify cancellation eligibility and call an API to cancel it. Which capability fits?The workflow must execute authorized actions.
Example 2An application turns a travel request into tool calls that check availability and make an approved reservation. Which capability fits?It coordinates and executes actions through tools.
Example 3A user asks an assistant to update a record after confirming the current value. What capability enables actual execution?An agent can invoke authorized read and update tools.
Example 4An AI system decides which tool to call, uses the result, and proceeds to the next step. Which pattern fits?Tool-based task execution is agentic behaviour.
Example 5A company wants a generative assistant to perform an approved inventory lookup and submit a reorder request. Which capability fits?It must act through business-system APIs.
Example 6A workflow needs reasoning over tool results before choosing the next authorized action. Which AI application pattern fits?An agent uses tools and intermediate results to complete a task.

ROUGE

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningMeasure overlap between generated text and reference text, commonly for summaries.Automatic comparison of summaries against reference summaries.
Common trapOverlap alone cannot establish factual correctness.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A team wants a common automatic overlap metric for generated versus reference summaries. Which metric fits?ROUGE is commonly used for summary overlap.
Example 2A summarization project measures how much reference content appears in candidate summaries using n-gram overlap. Which metric family fits?ROUGE evaluates reference overlap.
Example 3A developer needs a conventional summary-evaluation metric rather than a runtime measure. Which choice is most directly associated with summarization overlap?ROUGE is the summary-overlap metric.
Example 4A research team reports ROUGE-L based on sequence overlap with reference summaries. Which metric family is being used?ROUGE-L belongs to ROUGE.
Example 5A team compares a generated report summary against a human reference with an overlap-based metric. Which common metric fits?Reference summary overlap is a ROUGE use case.
Example 6A manager requests an automatic summary-overlap score alongside human factuality review. Which metric is a natural fit?ROUGE complements, but does not replace, factuality review.
Compare: BLEUCompare generated text with reference translations using modified n-gram precision and a brevity penalty.Use it when: Automatic translation quality comparison with references.
Compare: BERTScoreCompare candidate and reference text using contextual embedding similarity.Use it when: Assess semantic similarity beyond exact word overlap.
Compare: AccuracyThe fraction of all predictions that are correct, including both positive and negative classes.Use it when: Measure overall classification correctness when appropriate for the class distribution.

BLEU

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningCompare generated text with reference translations using modified n-gram precision and a brevity penalty.Automatic translation quality comparison with references.
Common trapA high BLEU score does not prove every translation is accurate or natural.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A translation team wants a conventional n-gram metric comparing machine translations with reference translations. Which metric fits?BLEU is commonly used for translation evaluation.
Example 2A report requests Bilingual Evaluation Understudy scores for translated sentences. Which metric is this?The expanded name identifies BLEU.
Example 3A team evaluates translation overlap and applies a brevity penalty to overly short candidates. Which metric fits?Modified n-gram precision and brevity penalty describe BLEU.
Example 4A company benchmarks machine-translated support articles against human translations with a standard translation metric. Which choice fits best?BLEU is the conventional reference-based translation metric here.
Example 5An evaluator chooses a translation metric based on matching n-grams rather than contextual embeddings. Which metric fits?BLEU uses n-gram overlap rather than semantic embedding similarity.
Example 6A localization project needs an automatic translation score in addition to human review of nuance. Which conventional metric fits?BLEU supports reference-based translation comparison.
Compare: ROUGEMeasure overlap between generated text and reference text, commonly for summaries.Use it when: Automatic comparison of summaries against reference summaries.
Compare: BERTScoreCompare candidate and reference text using contextual embedding similarity.Use it when: Assess semantic similarity beyond exact word overlap.
Compare: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)Square errors, average them and take the square root; larger errors receive greater weight.Use it when: Evaluate numerical regression predictions when large errors matter.

Example 2A team must compare answers for empathy and usefulness under a company-specific rubric. Which approach fits?People can assess contextual suitability using the rubric.
Example 3A legal summarizer has high overlap scores but may misrepresent obligations. Which additional evaluation is most important?Qualified reviewers should check meaning and factual fidelity.
Example 4A product team asks subject-matter experts to rank two model outputs for relevance. Which evaluation method is this?People are directly judging output quality.
Example 5A chatbot must be assessed for cultural sensitivity that simple overlap scores miss. Which approach fits?Human judgment addresses nuanced cultural context.
Example 6A company wants reviewers to inspect whether a summary faithfully reflects the original document. Which approach fits?Source-based human assessment can identify omissions and misrepresentations.

Compare: BLEUCompare generated text with reference translations using modified n-gram precision and a brevity penalty.Use it when: Automatic translation quality comparison with references.

Grounding and source validation

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningCompare generated claims with authorized supporting evidence and check whether the evidence supports the answer.Detect unsupported claims in RAG outputs.
Common trapA citation can be irrelevant or misleading; its presence alone is not proof.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A chatbot cites a policy but claims a refund period not present in that policy. What check should the team prioritize?Verify that each claim is supported by the cited evidence.
Example 2A RAG answer sounds fluent but invents a numerical amount. Which evaluation is most directly needed?Compare the amount with authoritative source content.
Example 3An assistant includes a source link but the link does not support its conclusion. What should be improved?Grounding evaluates support, not just citation presence.
Example 4A model answers even when retrieval finds no relevant evidence. Which safeguard should be added?Require sufficient support and an appropriate abstention path.
Example 5A team evaluates whether all important statements in generated summaries follow from the source documents. Which quality check is this?The focus is faithfulness to evidence.
Example 6A company wants to distinguish a plausible answer from a source-supported one. Which evaluation focus fits?Grounding and source validation test evidential support.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.
Compare: Supervised fine-tuningUpdate pretrained model weights using task-specific input–output examples.Use it when: Teach consistent task behaviour or style when prompting alone is inadequate and good training examples exist.
Compare: LatencyElapsed time to obtain a response, often measured per request or at a percentile.Use it when: Evaluate responsiveness for interactive applications.

Task completion rate

MeaningMeasure the proportion of attempted tasks successfully completed under a defined success criterion.Evaluate agent or workflow business outcomes.

Example 3An agent evaluation checks whether required actions were completed correctly rather than counting API calls. Which metric fits?Task completion measures end-to-end success.
Example 4A workflow assistant makes many tool calls but sometimes leaves work unfinished. Which metric should be prioritized?Completion rate captures whether the objective was achieved.
Example 5A company defines success as an approved ticket update with a verified tool result. Which metric tracks the fraction meeting that definition?Completion rate counts verified successful tasks.
Example 6An agent benchmark scores complete resolution of requests instead of answer fluency. Which metric matches?The outcome is successful task completion.

Scenario atlas — Domain 4: Responsible AI

Fairness and subgroup evaluation

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningAssess whether outcomes create inappropriate disparities across relevant groups.Inspect performance and error rates across demographic or operational subgroups.
Common trapFairness is contextual; equal overall accuracy does not prove fair outcomes.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.

Example 2A speech model works much worse for some accents than others. Which responsible-AI concern should the team assess?Performance differences across groups require fairness and inclusivity review.
Example 3A loan model has acceptable average accuracy but very different false-negative rates across groups. Which assessment is needed?Subgroup evaluation reveals unequal errors hidden by averages.
Example 4An image dataset underrepresents some skin tones. Which concern motivates improving representation and evaluating subgroup performance?Unrepresentative data can produce unfair outcomes.
Example 5A team reports only one overall score for a model used across diverse populations. Which additional assessment would help identify inappropriate disparities?Compare relevant subgroup outcomes and error rates.
Example 6A company asks whether similarly situated people receive appropriately consistent decisions. Which responsible-AI dimension is being assessed?The focus is fairness in treatment and outcomes.
Compare: RobustnessMaintain useful performance under reasonable variations, noise or unexpected inputs.Use it when: Test resilience to typos, image changes or distribution shifts within intended use.
Compare: SafetyReduce the potential for harmful outcomes from AI use.Use it when: Evaluate dangerous recommendations and implement appropriate safeguards.
Compare: LatencyElapsed time to obtain a response, often measured per request or at a percentile.Use it when: Evaluate responsiveness for interactive applications.

Robustness

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningMaintain useful performance under reasonable variations, noise or unexpected inputs.Test resilience to typos, image changes or distribution shifts within intended use.
Common trapRobustness is not merely understanding input and does not guarantee universal accuracy.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1A classifier fails after small lighting changes in photographs. Which responsible-AI property needs improvement?Robustness concerns stability under input variation.
Example 2A chatbot becomes unreliable when users make ordinary spelling mistakes. Which property should be tested?Reasonable input noise should not destroy performance.
Example 3A vision model must handle camera noise and modest changes in viewing angle. Which quality is the focus?The model needs resilience to variations.
Example 4An AI service works on clean examples but collapses on slightly corrupted inputs. Which property is weak?Sensitivity to small input changes indicates poor robustness.
Example 5A team evaluates a model on realistic noisy data in addition to clean benchmark data. Which property is it probing?The tests assess resilience outside ideal conditions.
Example 6An assistant should keep working when users paraphrase instructions in expected ways. Which quality is being assessed?Robust behaviour should tolerate reasonable phrasing variation.
Compare: Fairness and subgroup evaluationAssess whether outcomes create inappropriate disparities across relevant groups.Use it when: Inspect performance and error rates across demographic or operational subgroups.
Compare: ExplainabilityMake reasons behind predictions understandable to the intended audience.Use it when: Support informed review, debugging and decisions with meaningful explanations.
Compare: Privacy protectionMinimize inappropriate collection, use or exposure of personal information.Use it when: Restrict data access, minimize collection and apply suitable de-identification.

Explainability

MeaningMake reasons behind predictions understandable to the intended audience.Support informed review, debugging and decisions with meaningful explanations.

Example 2A developer wants to identify which inputs influenced a prediction. Which responsible-AI concern does this address?Explanation helps reveal model behaviour.
Example 3A complex model has strong predictive performance but users cannot understand its outputs. Which property should be improved?Explainability addresses understanding individual or overall predictions.
Example 4A team tailors model explanations for nontechnical case reviewers. Which design objective is this?Explanations should suit their human audience.
Example 5A company uses feature-attribution tools to help investigate unexpected predictions. Which quality is it improving?Feature attributions can support explainability and debugging.
Example 6A model explanation helps a reviewer challenge a decision rather than accept it blindly. Which quality is being supported?Understandable reasons enable informed human oversight.
Compare: Privacy protectionMinimize inappropriate collection, use or exposure of personal information.Use it when: Restrict data access, minimize collection and apply suitable de-identification.
Compare: RobustnessMaintain useful performance under reasonable variations, noise or unexpected inputs.Use it when: Test resilience to typos, image changes or distribution shifts within intended use.
Compare: ThroughputThe amount of work completed per unit time.Use it when: Measure requests per second or documents processed per hour.

Sustainability-aware model selection

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningMeet quality requirements while considering compute, energy and resource use.Choose an adequate efficient model and avoid unnecessary work.
Common trapThe largest model is not automatically the best choice; measure task quality and resource trade-offs.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1Two models meet the quality target. One uses substantially less compute for the same workload. Which selection principle supports choosing it?Adequate quality with less resource use supports sustainability.
Example 2A company removes redundant generation calls while preserving user outcomes. Which responsible selection concern does this support?Avoiding unnecessary computation reduces resource use.
Example 3A team chooses a smaller evaluated model instead of a larger one when both satisfy the task requirements. Which principle fits?Model size should be justified by quality needs and resource trade-offs.
Example 4An AI project includes energy and compute requirements in model comparisons. Which concern is being assessed?Environmental and resource impacts are sustainability factors.
Example 5A company avoids training from scratch when an existing model meets its needs after evaluation. Which principle supports the decision?Reusing adequate models can avoid unnecessary resource consumption.
Example 6A workload review considers caching safe repeated work to reduce repeated inference. Which responsible-AI consideration benefits?Reduced redundant computation can support sustainability.
Compare: Always choose the largest modelAssumes model size alone determines suitability, which is not reliable.Use it when: A larger model may be justified when measured task quality requires it, not simply because it is larger.
Compare: Increase training epochsTrain for additional complete passes through the dataset.Use it when: Consider when learning is incomplete and validation performance continues to improve; it can worsen overfitting.
Compare: Require manual review of every outputAdds human effort to all predictions regardless of risk.Use it when: Full review may suit a small high-impact workflow, but is not automatically efficient or sustainable.

Example 3A team gives reviewers relevant evidence and authority to reject AI recommendations. Which practice is being implemented?Human oversight must be informed and effective.
Example 4An organization publishes a route for users to contest automated decisions. Which responsible practice fits?Contestability enables correction and accountability.
Example 5A generative assistant proposes a consequential action but requires authorized human approval before execution. Which design practice fits?Human approval provides control over high-impact actions.
Example 6A company trains reviewers and tracks whether their interventions improve outcomes rather than merely collecting approvals. Which principle fits?Meaningful oversight is more than a nominal review step.

Compare: NAT gatewayAllow appropriate outbound connectivity from private-subnet resources to external destinations.Use it when: Provide internet egress without directly exposing the private resource to unsolicited inbound connections.
Compare: IAM least-privilege roles and policiesAuthorize only required actions on required resources for the correct principal.Use it when: Restrict human, application or service access using appropriate roles and policies.
Compare: Amazon CloudFrontDeliver content through a global content-delivery network.Use it when: Reduce latency when distributing web content to geographically dispersed users.

Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
MeaningApply supported controls to agent tool actions outside the model's free-form reasoning.Enforce which actions an agent may perform through supported integrations.
Common trapPrompt instructions alone are not a reliable authorization boundary; use actual policy enforcement.Identify what the scenario actually requires before choosing.
Example 1An agent may propose a tool call, but the application needs a separate enforceable policy deciding whether the action is allowed. Which AgentCore capability fits?Policy controls tool actions outside model-generated reasoning.
Example 2A company needs supported agent-tool restrictions enforced independently of a prompt that says “do not do this.” Which capability fits?AgentCore Policy applies external action controls.
Example 3An organization wants policies governing allowed tool operations in a supported AgentCore workflow. Which capability fits?The concern is authorization of agent actions.
Example 4A team needs deterministic policy checks before an agent's proposed tool action can proceed. Which AgentCore capability fits?Policy enforcement evaluates action permission separately from generation.
Example 5A business restricts an agent's supported tool operations according to centrally defined rules. Which capability is most directly relevant?AgentCore Policy governs tool action boundaries.
Example 6A system distinguishes safe response wording from whether a tool action is permitted. Which AgentCore capability addresses the latter?Tool authorization belongs to policy controls rather than content filtering.
Compare: Bedrock GuardrailsApply configured content, topic, sensitive-information and other supported safeguards to model interactions.Use it when: Help filter harmful content and enforce appropriate application boundaries.
Compare: Agent memoryRetain useful session or longer-lived information to support later interactions.Use it when: Remember relevant preferences or earlier task state under appropriate privacy controls.
Compare: TemperatureAdjust sampling randomness in generated outputs.Use it when: Make phrasing more predictable at lower settings or more varied at higher settings, where supported.

Official scope: AWS domain 5 objectives.

Uploaded-test corrections and qualifications

These items remain in the website for learning, with their source keys visible. They are excluded from adjusted scoring because they contain ambiguity, outdated claims or oversimplifications. The correction is the rule to retain.

TopicSimple explanationExample / application
Test 1, question 1Transfer learning is the intended answer when knowledge from a pretrained task is adapted to a related task. The wording about models sharing latest insights is vague; it is not a standard definition of cross-model optimization.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 3Low accuracy alone does not establish which training change is best. More epochs may help incomplete training, but may worsen overfitting. Inspect training and validation behaviour first.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 13The intended distinction is self-supervised pretraining versus supervised fine-tuning. Fine-tuning is not universally supervised; customization methods vary.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 18Temperature directly adjusts sampling randomness. Top P changes the cumulative-probability candidate pool and can also influence variety. Neither guarantees creativity or truth, so the broad wording is somewhat overlapping.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 21Both suitable hyperparameter changes and more representative training data can help overfitting. The question does not establish one universally most effective option.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 22This key is defective: labelled document classification and linear regression are supervised examples. Neural networks are architectures that can be trained with different learning approaches, not inherently supervised.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 25The broad statement that Amazon Q never permits model selection is outdated: supported Q Developer IDE experiences have model choices. Bedrock remains the platform for building custom FM applications.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 26Reward-driven learning fits the intended RL answer, but ongoing improvement does not uniquely imply RL. Supervised training from curated conversations can also improve a chatbot; ordinary inference does not automatically retrain it.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 27Read fine-tuning here as supervised fine-tuning. Continued pretraining commonly uses unlabelled domain text, but not every possible fine-tuning method requires manually labelled pairs.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 29Guardrails can help filter supported sensitive information but cannot guarantee that all confidential information is removed. Avoid training on secrets unnecessarily and layer access, data and output controls.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 31Top P is a cumulative probability threshold, not a percentage of vocabulary items. The key uses imprecise wording.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 41This is the historical Forecast demand-forecasting use case. Amazon Forecast is not available to new customers; treat this as a legacy course item rather than a new-service recommendation.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 45OpenSearch Serverless has been a common quick-create option, but supported defaults and storage choices evolve. Learn the vector-store role rather than an unconditional default.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 46Provisioned Throughput reserves inference capacity; it is not the fine-tuning operation. Supported custom models can also have on-demand deployment options. This question mixes customization with serving.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 1, question 53JumpStart provides pretrained models and solutions, but customization support is model-dependent; not every model is fully customizable in every way.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 4Sentiment analysis and fraud detection can use different learning methods. They are semi-supervised only when labelled and unlabelled examples are used together. Task names alone do not establish the answer.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 14The source key is outdated: Q Developer cost analysis supports visualizations in supported experiences. Treat its capabilities as evolving rather than memorising a prohibition on charts.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 26Multimodal embeddings support representation, matching and retrieval, but do not generate the conversational answer by themselves. The question does not establish total cost, so a unique most-cost-effective full chatbot architecture is not justified.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 32ChatGPT is an application associated with Transformer-based language models, not itself the name of a single architecture. Adobe Firefly and DALL-E are image-generation product/model families whose architectures vary; use them for visual generation rather than treating product names as precise architectural definitions.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 39Modern GenAI commonly uses deep learning, but a strict universal nesting of all generative AI inside deep learning is an oversimplification. AI contains ML, and deep learning is a subset of ML.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 45Poisoning means corrupting training or retrieval data. A bad response alone does not prove that poisoning occurred. Exposure or prompt leakage describes disclosure; diagnose the mechanism from evidence.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 48A multimodal model supports multiple modalities, but supported input and output combinations depend on the model. Image input does not imply image or audio generation.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 54Supported custom models can use appropriate on-demand or provisioned options. Smaller models are often cheaper for a given task, but actual cost depends on provider pricing, efficiency and workload.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 55A separate fixed validation split is optional when another validation method such as cross-validation is used. Validation also estimates generalization during development; a test set provides final independent evaluation, not hyperparameter tuning.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 2, question 61Higher temperature can increase variation and hallucination risk in some tasks, but it does not create a universal monotonic relationship. Temperature zero can still hallucinate. The supplied key is a simplified intended answer.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 6CNNs learn spatial image features and can process video frames. RNNs model sequences and can help with temporal analysis. A CNN-plus-RNN video pipeline is possible, so “CNN only image / RNN only video” is not an exclusive rule.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 7Diffusion models generally learn a reverse denoising process. The source wording about controlled random changes is vague; latent-space techniques are not exclusive to one model family.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 19Feature selection based on personal beliefs is a direct example of human-introduced bias, but biased historical hiring data also reflects human/social bias. The question does not make these mutually exclusive.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 25Selection chooses existing features; extraction transforms representations. Some extraction methods reduce dimensions, but not all feature extraction necessarily reduces feature count.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 34Sensitive disclosure is exposure. Prompt injection requires untrusted instructions that redirect behaviour; seeing a harmful suggestion in an output alone does not establish the cause.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 37Lambda and Rekognition are unambiguously regional here. WAF can have regional or CloudFront/global scope, so it is not universally one or the other.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 44Human review is useful for nuanced summary quality, but ROUGE/reference evaluation and benchmark testing are also valid. Without a specified quality criterion, human evaluation is not the uniquely best method.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 46Hijacking redirects an intended task; jailbreaking tries to bypass safety constraints. These can overlap, and response text alone is insufficient to prove the attack mechanism.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 57Human evaluation is useful for nuanced criteria and automatic evaluation for repeatable metrics. This is not an absolute qualitative/quantitative division: humans can assign numeric ratings and LLM judges can evaluate qualitative criteria.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 59Deep learning can learn features from raw inputs, but still often requires preprocessing and feature-design choices. Traditional ML can also use automated feature extraction.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 63Least-privilege service roles help, but do not alone guarantee answer isolation. Also restrict which knowledge base/collection a caller may query and enforce document/retrieval authorization. A user role does not automatically constrain a broad service role.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 3, question 65The three conventional main paradigms are supervised learning, unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning. Deep learning is a model family/technique, not a substitute for reinforcement learning. None of the listed options states the standard trio.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 4, question 8Model Cards document intended use and limitations. They can also include custom information within their prescribed schema, so the separate claim that cards can be customized is not inherently false.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 4, question 34LLMs commonly use nondeterministic sampling, but behaviour depends on settings and infrastructure. Do not treat every possible LLM configuration as necessarily nondeterministic.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 4, question 37Defensive prompt templates can help, but are not a reliable security boundary alone. Layer authorization, restricted tools, untrusted-input handling and output checks. Fixed responses may constrain risks but remove much generative utility.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 4, question 41GANs are a possible synthetic-data technique, not the only one. Synthetic data does not automatically protect privacy: assess memorization, leakage and representativeness.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 4, question 42Textract extracts document content (2); Forecast predicts future time-series outcomes (3); Kendra searches enterprise information (1). The correct mapping is A-2, B-3, C-1. Forecast is retained as a legacy course use case; new-customer access is closed.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 4, question 47Ground Truth Plus can provide managed labelling and quality assurance. It does not guarantee perfect annotation; suitable expert review may also be appropriate.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 4, question 52Forecast is a legacy service unavailable to new customers. Learn the forecasting use case, but check current options for a new implementation.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.
Test 4, question 59Prompt instructions alone cannot guarantee prevention of jailbreaks or prompt injection. Treat them as one layer, not an authorization or safety boundary.Read the original item alongside this qualification. Do not treat an answer key as a universal rule.

Your uploaded reference supplies Sections 1–8. The rest consolidates our lessons and fills the gaps against the AWS guide. Examples are illustrative, not real exam questions or actual quoted prices. Course section introductions and slide downloads are navigation, not separate technical exam objectives. Exact quotas, supported languages, model availability and prices should be checked for a real deployment; memorising their changing details is not the purpose of these notes.
